title: The Peasant Who Invented Chinese Meritocracy
event_summary: Emperor Yang of Sui, acting on proposals from his minister Yang Su and lower-ranking officials from non-aristocratic backgrounds, formally institutionalized the imperial examination system (keju) in 605 AD at the eastern capital of Luoyang. For the first time in any civilization, government positions were systematically awarded based on standardized written tests rather than birth, wealth, or military prowess. Candidates from farming villages sat alongside sons of minor gentry, answering questions on statecraft, ethics, and classical literature to earn bureaucratic appointments.
why_forgotten: Emperor Yang is remembered almost exclusively as a tyrant whose extravagance collapsed the Sui Dynasty, so his administrative innovations are overshadowed by moralistic condemnation. The Tang Dynasty, which perfected and expanded the examination system, typically receives credit for it, erasing the Sui origins. Western historiography also tends to treat Chinese bureaucratic history as a monolithic, unchanging tradition rather than highlighting its revolutionary founding moment.
why_it_matters: The keju system ran for over 1,300 years and became the world's first large-scale meritocratic institution, directly inspiring the civil service examinations adopted by the British Empire in the 1850s after East India Company officials studied it. Every modern government that hires through standardized testing—from the U.S. federal civil service to the French concours system—traces its philosophical DNA to this 605 AD innovation. The radical idea that competence, not bloodline, should determine who governs remains the bedrock assumption of modern democratic administration worldwide.
